pdf-figure-1-1-1.title: Velocity and distance readings
pdf-figure-1-1-1.text: A speedometer measures instantaneous speed, while the odometer records accumulated distance.
pdf-figure-1-1-1.caption: Velocity and distance readings

pdf-figure-1-3-1.title: Slopes and initial values
pdf-figure-1-3-1.text: Changing a line's intercept changes its starting value; changing its slope changes its rate of change.
pdf-figure-1-3-1.caption: Slopes and initial values

pdf-figure-1-5-1.title: Domain and range of linear functions
pdf-figure-1-5-1.text: The horizontal interval gives the domain, and the corresponding vertical interval gives the range.
pdf-figure-1-5-1.caption: Domain and range of linear functions

pdf-figure-1-6-1.title: Scaling the input or the output
pdf-figure-1-6-1.text: Scaling a function's input and scaling its output can produce different intercepts even when their slopes agree.
pdf-figure-1-6-1.caption: Scaling the input or the output

pdf-figure-1-7-1.title: Signed velocity intervals
pdf-figure-1-7-1.text: Positive and negative velocity intervals contribute opposite signed changes in displacement.
pdf-figure-1-7-1.caption: Signed velocity intervals

pdf-figure-1-7-2.title: Reading motion from distance graphs
pdf-figure-1-7-2.text: Rising, falling and horizontal portions of a distance graph indicate different velocities.
pdf-figure-1-7-2.caption: Reading motion from distance graphs

pdf-figure-1-7-3.title: Velocity pulses
pdf-figure-1-7-3.text: The width and height of each velocity pulse determine its contribution to displacement.
pdf-figure-1-7-3.caption: Velocity pulses

pdf-figure-1-7-4.title: Slopes of piecewise distance graphs
pdf-figure-1-7-4.text: Each straight segment of a distance graph has a constant velocity given by its slope.
pdf-figure-1-7-4.caption: Slopes of piecewise distance graphs

pdf-figure-1-7-5.title: Comparing linear distance models
pdf-figure-1-7-5.text: The starting value and the slope must both be read when comparing two distance models.
pdf-figure-1-7-5.caption: Comparing linear distance models

pdf-figure-1-12-1.title: Recovering distance from velocity
pdf-figure-1-12-1.text: Accumulated signed area under a piecewise constant velocity graph produces a piecewise linear distance graph.
pdf-figure-1-12-1.caption: Recovering distance from velocity

pdf-figure-1-14-1.title: Piecewise rates and accumulated totals
pdf-figure-1-14-1.text: Constant rates on successive intervals create connected linear segments in the accumulated total.
pdf-figure-1-14-1.caption: Piecewise rates and accumulated totals

pdf-figure-1-15-1.title: Differences and accumulated sums
pdf-figure-1-15-1.text: Step heights represent discrete changes, while successive sums reconstruct the accumulated values.
pdf-figure-1-15-1.caption: Differences and accumulated sums

pdf-figure-1-17-1.title: Secants approaching a tangent
pdf-figure-1-17-1.text: As the time increment decreases, the average velocity approaches the slope of the tangent.
pdf-figure-1-17-1.caption: Secants approaching a tangent

pdf-figure-1-20-2.title: Secants, tangents and velocity graphs
pdf-figure-1-20-2.text: The first diagram compares a secant with a tangent; the remaining diagrams distinguish distance graphs from velocity graphs.
pdf-figure-1-20-2.caption: Secants, tangents and velocity graphs

pdf-figure-1-23-1.title: Sine and cosine over a full revolution
pdf-figure-1-23-1.text: The trigonometric graphs relate angular position on a circle to periodic horizontal and vertical coordinates.
pdf-figure-1-23-1.caption: Sine and cosine over a full revolution

pdf-figure-1-24-1.title: Position and velocity on a circle
pdf-figure-1-24-1.text: The velocity vector is tangent to the circular path and perpendicular to the radius.
pdf-figure-1-24-1.caption: Position and velocity on a circle

pdf-figure-1-25-1.title: Vertical motion on a circle
pdf-figure-1-25-1.text: The vertical coordinate and the vertical component of velocity vary with the angular position.
pdf-figure-1-25-1.caption: Vertical motion on a circle

pdf-figure-1-26-1.title: Harmonic motion and its derivative
pdf-figure-1-26-1.text: The sine curve and its cosine derivative explain when height increases, decreases or reaches a turning point.
pdf-figure-1-26-1.caption: Harmonic motion and its derivative

pdf-figure-1-30-1.title: Trigonometric ratios
pdf-figure-1-30-1.text: The horizontal coordinate, vertical coordinate and radius determine the basic trigonometric ratios.
pdf-figure-1-30-1.caption: Trigonometric ratios

pdf-figure-1-30-2.title: Angles and trigonometric periods
pdf-figure-1-30-2.text: A full turn corresponds to a full period; doubling the angle changes the period of the resulting oscillation.
pdf-figure-1-30-2.caption: Angles and trigonometric periods

pdf-figure-1-32-1.title: Tangent, secant and cosecant
pdf-figure-1-32-1.text: The diagrams interpret trigonometric ratios as slopes and lengths associated with a point on the unit circle.
pdf-figure-1-32-1.caption: Tangent, secant and cosecant

pdf-figure-1-33-1.title: Special angles
pdf-figure-1-33-1.text: Standard right triangles and the unit circle determine exact trigonometric values at special angles.
pdf-figure-1-33-1.caption: Special angles

pdf-figure-1-35-1.title: Sampling a sine curve
pdf-figure-1-35-1.text: Plotting values only at selected sample points can produce large-scale patterns that differ from the continuous curve.
pdf-figure-1-35-1.caption: Sampling a sine curve

pdf-figure-1-36-1.title: Patterns in sampled data
pdf-figure-1-36-1.text: Different sampling scales reveal apparent curves and repeating patterns in the same oscillatory data.
pdf-figure-1-36-1.caption: Patterns in sampled data

pdf-figure-2-3-1.title: Derivative at a corner
pdf-figure-2-3-1.text: The distance graph changes slope abruptly at the corner, so the derivative does not exist there.
pdf-figure-2-3-1.caption: Derivative at a corner

pdf-figure-2-4-1.title: Average slope and tangent slope
pdf-figure-2-4-1.text: The secant gives an average rate over an interval, while the tangent gives the rate at one point.
pdf-figure-2-4-1.caption: Average slope and tangent slope

pdf-figure-2-4-2.title: A reciprocal function and its derivative
pdf-figure-2-4-2.text: The reciprocal graph decreases, and its derivative records a negative slope whose magnitude depends on position.
pdf-figure-2-4-2.caption: A reciprocal function and its derivative

pdf-figure-2-7-1.title: Difference quotients
pdf-figure-2-7-1.text: The change in a function value over an interval determines the secant slope used in the derivative definition.
pdf-figure-2-7-1.caption: Difference quotients

pdf-figure-2-7-2.title: Reading changes from graphs
pdf-figure-2-7-2.text: Differences between plotted values can be compared with the slopes of the intervening segments.
pdf-figure-2-7-2.caption: Reading changes from graphs

pdf-figure-2-12-1.title: Marginal and average quantities
pdf-figure-2-12-1.text: Slopes describe marginal changes, while ratios to the input describe average quantities.
pdf-figure-2-12-1.caption: Marginal and average quantities

pdf-figure-2-16-1.title: Zooming in on a smooth curve
pdf-figure-2-16-1.text: Successive magnifications make a smooth curve look increasingly like its tangent line.
pdf-figure-2-16-1.caption: Zooming in on a smooth curve

pdf-figure-2-18-1.title: Tangents, normals and motion
pdf-figure-2-18-1.text: A tangent records local direction; a normal is perpendicular to it, and motion graphs provide related slope examples.
pdf-figure-2-18-1.caption: Tangents, normals and motion

pdf-figure-2-20-1.title: Nearby secant lines
pdf-figure-2-20-1.text: Secants through nearby points approach the tangent as their second point moves toward the point of contact.
pdf-figure-2-20-1.caption: Nearby secant lines

pdf-figure-2-22-1.title: Parabolas and reciprocal curves
pdf-figure-2-22-1.text: The plotted geometry connects tangent directions with familiar algebraic curves.
pdf-figure-2-22-1.caption: Parabolas and reciprocal curves

pdf-figure-2-24-1.title: Small-angle geometry
pdf-figure-2-24-1.text: Geometric comparisons near the origin support the limits used to differentiate sine and cosine.
pdf-figure-2-24-1.caption: Small-angle geometry

pdf-figure-2-24-2.title: The sine difference quotient
pdf-figure-2-24-2.text: The slope of a short secant on the sine curve approaches the cosine value at the point.
pdf-figure-2-24-2.caption: The sine difference quotient

pdf-figure-2-25-1.title: Small-angle trigonometric functions
pdf-figure-2-25-1.text: Sine, tangent and their small-angle ratios have closely related behavior near the origin.
pdf-figure-2-25-1.caption: Small-angle trigonometric functions

pdf-figure-2-25-2.title: Comparing a sector with triangles
pdf-figure-2-25-2.text: Areas of a sector and neighboring triangles provide bounds for the small-angle sine limit.
pdf-figure-2-25-2.caption: Comparing a sector with triangles

pdf-figure-2-27-1.title: Signs of trigonometric slopes
pdf-figure-2-27-1.text: Increasing and decreasing portions of sine and cosine correspond to the signs of their derivatives.
pdf-figure-2-27-1.caption: Signs of trigonometric slopes

pdf-figure-2-31-1.title: The product rule by area
pdf-figure-2-31-1.text: A small change in a rectangle's area can be separated into contributions from changing each side.
pdf-figure-2-31-1.caption: The product rule by area

pdf-figure-2-32-1.title: Changes in a ratio
pdf-figure-2-32-1.text: A triangle diagram relates changes in numerator and denominator to the resulting ratio.
pdf-figure-2-32-1.caption: Changes in a ratio

pdf-figure-2-32-2.title: Normalized ratio geometry
pdf-figure-2-32-2.text: Rescaling the triangle helps compare a quotient before and after a small change.
pdf-figure-2-32-2.caption: Normalized ratio geometry

pdf-figure-2-34-1.title: The power rule by geometry
pdf-figure-2-34-1.text: Changes in area and volume illustrate why differentiating powers introduces a coefficient.
pdf-figure-2-34-1.caption: The power rule by geometry

pdf-figure-2-35-1.title: Fractional powers at the origin
pdf-figure-2-35-1.text: Fractional-power curves can have zero or infinite tangent slope at the origin.
pdf-figure-2-35-1.caption: Fractional powers at the origin

pdf-figure-2-37-1.title: Limit bounds
pdf-figure-2-37-1.text: Horizontal and vertical bands express how controlling the input keeps function values close to a limit.
pdf-figure-2-37-1.caption: Limit bounds

pdf-figure-2-38-1.title: Limits and shrinking intervals
pdf-figure-2-38-1.text: The diagrams compare bounds and successive approximations to illustrate convergence.
pdf-figure-2-38-1.caption: Limits and shrinking intervals

pdf-figure-2-41-1.title: Different types of limiting behavior
pdf-figure-2-41-1.text: The graphs distinguish finite limits, discontinuities and behavior that prevents a limit from existing.
pdf-figure-2-41-1.caption: Different types of limiting behavior

pdf-figure-2-45-1.title: Continuity and discontinuity
pdf-figure-2-45-1.text: Jumps, missing values and oscillations illustrate different ways continuity can fail.
pdf-figure-2-45-1.caption: Continuity and discontinuity

pdf-figure-3-2-1.title: A tangent approximation
pdf-figure-3-2-1.text: The tangent line provides a nearby linear estimate to a curved function.
pdf-figure-3-2-1.caption: A tangent approximation

pdf-figure-3-4-1.title: Differential and actual change
pdf-figure-3-4-1.text: The tangent predicts the differential, while the curve gives the actual change in function value.
pdf-figure-3-4-1.caption: Differential and actual change

pdf-figure-3-7-1.title: Stationary points and derivatives
pdf-figure-3-7-1.text: Zeros of the first derivative identify candidates for local extrema, whose behavior is checked on the graph.
pdf-figure-3-7-1.caption: Stationary points and derivatives

pdf-figure-3-9-1.title: Local and absolute extrema
pdf-figure-3-9-1.text: A local extremum compares nearby values, while an absolute extremum compares values over the whole domain.
pdf-figure-3-9-1.caption: Local and absolute extrema

pdf-figure-3-11-1.title: Optimization through rates
pdf-figure-3-11-1.text: Competing travel times and their slopes determine an optimal choice.
pdf-figure-3-11-1.caption: Optimization through rates

pdf-figure-3-12-1.title: Costs, energy and optimization
pdf-figure-3-12-1.text: Different applications lead to functions whose derivatives locate possible optimal values.
pdf-figure-3-12-1.caption: Costs, energy and optimization

pdf-figure-3-14-1.title: Geometric and economic objectives
pdf-figure-3-14-1.text: A diagram helps express the quantity to optimize in terms of a single variable.
pdf-figure-3-14-1.caption: Geometric and economic objectives

pdf-figure-3-14-2.title: Optimizing dimensions
pdf-figure-3-14-2.text: Geometric constraints reduce the number of independent dimensions before differentiation.
pdf-figure-3-14-2.caption: Optimizing dimensions

pdf-figure-3-15-1.title: Reflection and refraction paths
pdf-figure-3-15-1.text: Comparing path lengths and travel costs explains why optimal paths obey geometric conditions.
pdf-figure-3-15-1.caption: Reflection and refraction paths

pdf-figure-3-17-1.title: Curvature and the second derivative
pdf-figure-3-17-1.text: The sign of the second derivative describes how the slope changes and how the curve bends.
pdf-figure-3-17-1.caption: Curvature and the second derivative

pdf-figure-3-21-1.title: Linear and quadratic approximations
pdf-figure-3-21-1.text: Adding a quadratic term can reproduce bending that a tangent line alone cannot capture.
pdf-figure-3-21-1.caption: Linear and quadratic approximations

pdf-figure-3-24-1.title: Reading a heart-rate scale
pdf-figure-3-24-1.text: The reference scale relates the spacing of repeated recorded cycles to heart rate.
pdf-figure-3-24-1.caption: Reading a heart-rate scale

pdf-figure-3-24-2.title: Features of a recorded waveform
pdf-figure-3-24-2.text: Peaks, timing and repeated patterns provide information that can be read from a measured graph.
pdf-figure-3-24-2.caption: Features of a recorded waveform

pdf-figure-3-25-1.title: Recording electrical activity
pdf-figure-3-25-1.text: The heart and electrode diagram explains the physical source of the plotted electrical signals.
pdf-figure-3-25-1.caption: Recording electrical activity

pdf-figure-3-26-1.title: Comparing waveforms
pdf-figure-3-26-1.text: Different recorded waveforms show why shape, timing and repeated features matter when interpreting a graph.
pdf-figure-3-26-1.caption: Comparing waveforms

pdf-figure-3-27-1.title: Qualitative curve sketches
pdf-figure-3-27-1.text: Intercepts, asymptotes, extrema and bending work together to determine a plausible curve.
pdf-figure-3-27-1.caption: Qualitative curve sketches

pdf-figure-3-29-1.title: Zooming near an optimum
pdf-figure-3-29-1.text: Changing the plotting scale reveals the local shape of a function near its minimum.
pdf-figure-3-29-1.caption: Zooming near an optimum

pdf-figure-3-30-1.title: Slope crossing zero
pdf-figure-3-30-1.text: A negative-to-positive change in slope indicates a local minimum.
pdf-figure-3-30-1.caption: Slope crossing zero

pdf-figure-3-31-1.title: The effect of plotting scale
pdf-figure-3-31-1.text: The apparent angle of a line changes with the scale, even though its mathematical slope is fixed.
pdf-figure-3-31-1.caption: The effect of plotting scale

pdf-figure-3-34-1.title: Conic sections
pdf-figure-3-34-1.text: Different cutting planes through a cone produce the standard conic curves.
pdf-figure-3-34-1.caption: Conic sections

pdf-figure-3-35-1.title: Parabolas and focal geometry
pdf-figure-3-35-1.text: The focus and directrix determine a parabola and help describe its tangent geometry.
pdf-figure-3-35-1.caption: Parabolas and focal geometry

pdf-figure-3-37-1.title: Ellipses and their foci
pdf-figure-3-37-1.text: The sum of distances to two foci remains constant along an ellipse.
pdf-figure-3-37-1.caption: Ellipses and their foci

pdf-figure-3-39-1.title: Hyperbolas and asymptotes
pdf-figure-3-39-1.text: The two branches of a hyperbola approach straight asymptotes and have a focal description.
pdf-figure-3-39-1.caption: Hyperbolas and asymptotes

pdf-figure-3-42-1.title: Tangents to an ellipse
pdf-figure-3-42-1.text: The focal geometry of an ellipse constrains the direction of a tangent at a point.
pdf-figure-3-42-1.caption: Tangents to an ellipse

pdf-figure-3-45-1.title: Graphical fixed-point iteration
pdf-figure-3-45-1.text: Alternating between the function graph and the diagonal shows successive iterates.
pdf-figure-3-45-1.caption: Graphical fixed-point iteration

pdf-figure-3-46-1.title: Attracting and repelling fixed points
pdf-figure-3-46-1.text: The local slope of the iteration function helps explain whether nearby iterates move toward or away from a fixed point.
pdf-figure-3-46-1.caption: Attracting and repelling fixed points

pdf-figure-3-48-1.title: Improving an iteration
pdf-figure-3-48-1.text: Changing the iteration function can change convergence even when the desired fixed point remains the same.
pdf-figure-3-48-1.caption: Improving an iteration

pdf-figure-3-51-1.title: Newton steps from tangent lines
pdf-figure-3-51-1.text: Each tangent line gives a new estimate of the root through its horizontal-axis intercept.
pdf-figure-3-51-1.caption: Newton steps from tangent lines

pdf-figure-3-54-1.title: Sensitivity of iterative methods
pdf-figure-3-54-1.text: Different starting points and function shapes can lead to different iterative behavior.
pdf-figure-3-54-1.caption: Sensitivity of iterative methods

pdf-figure-3-57-1.title: Bifurcation patterns
pdf-figure-3-57-1.text: Varying an iteration parameter can change a stable fixed point into cycles and more complex behavior.
pdf-figure-3-57-1.caption: Bifurcation patterns

pdf-figure-3-57-2.title: Successive geometric constructions
pdf-figure-3-57-2.text: Repeated refinement builds increasingly detailed geometric patterns.
pdf-figure-3-57-2.caption: Successive geometric constructions

pdf-figure-3-61-1.title: The mean value theorem
pdf-figure-3-61-1.text: A tangent somewhere inside an interval has the same slope as the secant joining its endpoints.
pdf-figure-3-61-1.caption: The mean value theorem

pdf-figure-3-62-1.title: Rolle's theorem and equal slopes
pdf-figure-3-62-1.text: Endpoint conditions force a horizontal tangent in one case and a tangent parallel to a secant in another.
pdf-figure-3-62-1.caption: Rolle's theorem and equal slopes

pdf-figure-3-64-1.title: Comparing function changes
pdf-figure-3-64-1.text: The diagrams relate endpoint changes to slopes within the interval.
pdf-figure-3-64-1.caption: Comparing function changes

pdf-figure-3-67-1.title: Geometric limit comparisons
pdf-figure-3-67-1.text: Areas and bounding shapes provide geometric ways to compare limiting quantities.
pdf-figure-3-67-1.caption: Geometric limit comparisons

pdf-figure-4-2-1.title: Composing functions
pdf-figure-4-2-1.text: Changing the inner function changes the input supplied to the outer function.
pdf-figure-4-2-1.caption: Composing functions

pdf-figure-4-3-1.title: The chain rule through increments
pdf-figure-4-3-1.text: An input change passes through two functions, so the overall rate combines the two rates.
pdf-figure-4-3-1.caption: The chain rule through increments

pdf-figure-4-9-1.title: Related-rate geometry
pdf-figure-4-9-1.text: A fixed geometric relation connects changing lengths, allowing one rate to be found from another.
pdf-figure-4-9-1.caption: Related-rate geometry

pdf-figure-4-11-1.title: A moving point and a changing angle
pdf-figure-4-11-1.text: The triangle relates horizontal separation, height, distance and angle before their rates are compared.
pdf-figure-4-11-1.caption: A moving point and a changing angle

pdf-figure-4-12-1.title: Linked geometric quantities
pdf-figure-4-12-1.text: Lengths constrained by a mechanism or triangle cannot change independently.
pdf-figure-4-12-1.caption: Linked geometric quantities

pdf-figure-4-13-1.title: Inverse functions
pdf-figure-4-13-1.text: Reversing the roles of input and output reverses the action of a one-to-one function.
pdf-figure-4-13-1.caption: Inverse functions

pdf-figure-4-14-1.title: Restricting a domain for an inverse
pdf-figure-4-14-1.text: A function must be one-to-one on the chosen interval to define an inverse function.
pdf-figure-4-14-1.caption: Restricting a domain for an inverse

pdf-figure-4-15-1.title: Reciprocal slopes of inverse graphs
pdf-figure-4-15-1.text: Reflecting across the diagonal exchanges horizontal and vertical changes.
pdf-figure-4-15-1.caption: Reciprocal slopes of inverse graphs

pdf-figure-4-16-1.title: Exponential and logarithmic inverses
pdf-figure-4-16-1.text: An exponential graph and its logarithmic inverse illustrate reciprocal tangent slopes.
pdf-figure-4-16-1.caption: Exponential and logarithmic inverses

pdf-figure-4-17-1.title: Function and inverse composition
pdf-figure-4-17-1.text: Applying a function and then its inverse returns the original input on the appropriate domain.
pdf-figure-4-17-1.caption: Function and inverse composition

pdf-figure-4-20-1.title: The inverse sine derivative
pdf-figure-4-20-1.text: A right triangle and the unit circle relate the derivative of inverse sine to the original sine function.
pdf-figure-4-20-1.caption: The inverse sine derivative

pdf-figure-4-22-1.title: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
pdf-figure-4-22-1.text: The graphs illustrate how the slopes of inverse trigonometric functions vary across their domains.
pdf-figure-4-22-1.caption: Inverse trigonometric derivatives

pdf-figure-4-22-2.title: Inverse tangent and related curves
pdf-figure-4-22-2.text: The inverse tangent graph has a bounded range and a slope that decreases away from the origin.
pdf-figure-4-22-2.caption: Inverse tangent and related curves

pdf-figure-4-23-1.title: Triangles for inverse trigonometry
pdf-figure-4-23-1.text: A suitable right triangle turns inverse trigonometric expressions into ratios of side lengths.
pdf-figure-4-23-1.caption: Triangles for inverse trigonometry

pdf-figure-5-3-1.title: Accumulation with rectangles
pdf-figure-5-3-1.text: Adding rectangular contributions builds an accumulated total from successive rates.
pdf-figure-5-3-1.caption: Accumulation with rectangles

pdf-figure-5-4-1.title: Finer partitions
pdf-figure-5-4-1.text: Smaller intervals produce more rectangles and a closer approximation to accumulated area.
pdf-figure-5-4-1.caption: Finer partitions

pdf-figure-5-7-1.title: A rate and its accumulation
pdf-figure-5-7-1.text: The height of the rate curve determines how quickly the accumulated total changes.
pdf-figure-5-7-1.caption: A rate and its accumulation

pdf-figure-5-8-1.title: Area as a limit of sums
pdf-figure-5-8-1.text: Refining rectangular approximations leads to the definite integral.
pdf-figure-5-8-1.caption: Area as a limit of sums

pdf-figure-5-9-1.title: Recovering a function from its rate
pdf-figure-5-9-1.text: Positive and negative rates determine where the accumulated function rises or falls.
pdf-figure-5-9-1.caption: Recovering a function from its rate

pdf-figure-5-11-1.title: Rates with changing sign
pdf-figure-5-11-1.text: The sign and area of each part of a rate graph control the accumulated change.
pdf-figure-5-11-1.caption: Rates with changing sign

pdf-figure-5-11-2.title: Comparing rates and totals
pdf-figure-5-11-2.text: A rate graph and its accumulated total encode different but related information.
pdf-figure-5-11-2.caption: Comparing rates and totals

pdf-figure-5-15-1.title: Power sums and areas
pdf-figure-5-15-1.text: Sums of powers can be interpreted as geometric approximations to integrals.
pdf-figure-5-15-1.caption: Power sums and areas

pdf-figure-5-17-1.title: Geometric power sums
pdf-figure-5-17-1.text: Squares and cubes provide visual models for sums of powers.
pdf-figure-5-17-1.caption: Geometric power sums

pdf-figure-5-18-1.title: Error and computational work
pdf-figure-5-18-1.text: A numerical integration method balances its approximation error against the number of evaluations.
pdf-figure-5-18-1.caption: Error and computational work

pdf-figure-5-24-1.title: Substitution and accumulated area
pdf-figure-5-24-1.text: Changing variables transforms both the argument of the function and the differential.
pdf-figure-5-24-1.caption: Substitution and accumulated area

pdf-figure-5-28-1.title: Upper and lower sums
pdf-figure-5-28-1.text: Rectangles based on different heights bound or approximate the area under a curve.
pdf-figure-5-28-1.caption: Upper and lower sums

pdf-figure-5-29-1.title: Choices of rectangle heights
pdf-figure-5-29-1.text: Left, right, midpoint and extreme values lead to different integral approximations.
pdf-figure-5-29-1.caption: Choices of rectangle heights

pdf-figure-5-33-1.title: Additivity and signed area
pdf-figure-5-33-1.text: Integrals combine across intervals and retain the sign of the region relative to the axis.
pdf-figure-5-33-1.caption: Additivity and signed area

pdf-figure-5-33-2.title: Average height
pdf-figure-5-33-2.text: A constant height over an interval can have the same signed area as a varying function.
pdf-figure-5-33-2.caption: Average height

pdf-figure-5-34-1.title: Integral averages
pdf-figure-5-34-1.text: The average value depends on the signed area divided by the interval length.
pdf-figure-5-34-1.caption: Integral averages

pdf-figure-5-38-1.title: A geometric probability model
pdf-figure-5-38-1.text: Lengths and angles in the needle diagram determine whether a randomly placed segment crosses a line.
pdf-figure-5-38-1.caption: A geometric probability model

pdf-figure-5-40-1.title: The derivative of accumulated area
pdf-figure-5-40-1.text: A small extension of the interval adds a thin strip whose area is approximately height times width.
pdf-figure-5-40-1.caption: The derivative of accumulated area

pdf-figure-5-40-2.title: Changing integration limits
pdf-figure-5-40-2.text: Moving an endpoint adds or removes area at that endpoint.
pdf-figure-5-40-2.caption: Changing integration limits

pdf-figure-5-43-1.title: Thin rings and shells
pdf-figure-5-43-1.text: A thin geometric layer has area or volume approximated by its boundary measure times its thickness.
pdf-figure-5-43-1.caption: Thin rings and shells

pdf-figure-5-44-1.title: Differentials in geometry
pdf-figure-5-44-1.text: Small changes in geometric dimensions lead to first-order changes in areas and lengths.
pdf-figure-5-44-1.caption: Differentials in geometry

pdf-figure-5-45-1.title: Area elements in different coordinates
pdf-figure-5-45-1.text: Triangles and sectors illustrate different ways to describe a small area element.
pdf-figure-5-45-1.caption: Area elements in different coordinates

pdf-figure-5-45-2.title: Choosing an area element
pdf-figure-5-45-2.text: The geometry determines which variable and differential make an integral convenient.
pdf-figure-5-45-2.caption: Choosing an area element

pdf-figure-5-47-1.title: Trapezoidal approximation
pdf-figure-5-47-1.text: Replacing each short curve segment by a straight line gives a trapezoidal area estimate.
pdf-figure-5-47-1.caption: Trapezoidal approximation

pdf-figure-5-49-1.title: Numerical integration error
pdf-figure-5-49-1.text: The shape of the curve explains the discrepancy between a numerical rule and the true integral.
pdf-figure-5-49-1.caption: Numerical integration error

pdf-figure-5-51-1.title: Weighted quadrature rules
pdf-figure-5-51-1.text: Different patterns of weights combine sampled values into integral approximations.
pdf-figure-5-51-1.caption: Weighted quadrature rules

pdf-figure-6-3-1.title: A logarithmic scale
pdf-figure-6-3-1.text: Equal distances on a logarithmic scale represent equal multiplicative factors.
pdf-figure-6-3-1.caption: A logarithmic scale

pdf-figure-6-4-1.title: Exponentials and logarithms
pdf-figure-6-4-1.text: Exponential growth and its logarithmic inverse have different shapes and exchange input with output.
pdf-figure-6-4-1.caption: Exponentials and logarithms

pdf-figure-6-6-1.title: Straight lines on logarithmic axes
pdf-figure-6-6-1.text: A logarithmic change of scale can turn multiplicative relationships into straight lines.
pdf-figure-6-6-1.caption: Straight lines on logarithmic axes

pdf-figure-6-6-2.title: Powers on logarithmic axes
pdf-figure-6-6-2.text: The slope on a log-log plot represents the exponent of a power relationship.
pdf-figure-6-6-2.caption: Powers on logarithmic axes

pdf-figure-6-7-1.title: Slopes of exponential and logarithmic graphs
pdf-figure-6-7-1.text: Inverse graphs have reciprocal slopes at corresponding points.
pdf-figure-6-7-1.caption: Slopes of exponential and logarithmic graphs

pdf-figure-6-12-1.title: Exponential derivative relationships
pdf-figure-6-12-1.text: The derivative of an exponential is proportional to the original exponential.
pdf-figure-6-12-1.caption: Exponential derivative relationships

pdf-figure-6-17-1.title: Direction fields for growth
pdf-figure-6-17-1.text: Short line segments show the local slope required by a differential equation.
pdf-figure-6-17-1.caption: Direction fields for growth

pdf-figure-6-18-1.title: Growth, decay and compounding
pdf-figure-6-18-1.text: Different growth laws produce different long-term behavior even when their initial values agree.
pdf-figure-6-18-1.caption: Growth, decay and compounding

pdf-figure-6-21-1.title: Exponential approaches to equilibrium
pdf-figure-6-21-1.text: The sign of the rate determines whether a solution grows away from or decays toward an equilibrium.
pdf-figure-6-21-1.caption: Exponential approaches to equilibrium

pdf-figure-6-24-1.title: Growth models with shifted equilibria
pdf-figure-6-24-1.text: An added constant term changes the equilibrium around which exponential behavior occurs.
pdf-figure-6-24-1.caption: Growth models with shifted equilibria

pdf-figure-6-28-1.title: Logarithms as areas
pdf-figure-6-28-1.text: Area under the reciprocal curve provides a geometric definition of the natural logarithm.
pdf-figure-6-28-1.caption: Logarithms as areas

pdf-figure-6-30-1.title: The exponential and reciprocal area
pdf-figure-6-30-1.text: Scaling an endpoint under the reciprocal curve corresponds to changes in logarithmic area.
pdf-figure-6-30-1.caption: The exponential and reciprocal area

pdf-figure-6-30-2.title: A logarithmic curve and its slope
pdf-figure-6-30-2.text: The logarithm increases while its reciprocal derivative decreases.
pdf-figure-6-30-2.caption: A logarithmic curve and its slope

pdf-figure-6-30-3.title: Small changes and logarithmic area
pdf-figure-6-30-3.text: A narrow strip under the reciprocal curve gives the differential of the logarithm.
pdf-figure-6-30-3.caption: Small changes and logarithmic area

pdf-figure-6-36-1.title: Separable growth laws
pdf-figure-6-36-1.text: Different dependences on the current value can produce qualitatively different growth curves.
pdf-figure-6-36-1.caption: Separable growth laws

pdf-figure-6-38-1.title: Logistic saturation
pdf-figure-6-38-1.text: A logistic solution slows as it approaches a finite carrying capacity.
pdf-figure-6-38-1.caption: Logistic saturation

pdf-figure-6-39-1.title: Equilibria and direction of change
pdf-figure-6-39-1.text: The signs of the differential equation show how solutions move between equilibrium values.
pdf-figure-6-39-1.caption: Equilibria and direction of change

pdf-figure-6-40-1.title: Qualitative behavior of differential equations
pdf-figure-6-40-1.text: Direction and equilibrium information help predict a solution without explicitly solving the equation.
pdf-figure-6-40-1.caption: Qualitative behavior of differential equations

pdf-figure-6-47-1.title: Powers, decay and oscillation
pdf-figure-6-47-1.text: Different exponents or parameters can create growth, decay or oscillatory behavior.
pdf-figure-6-47-1.caption: Powers, decay and oscillation

pdf-figure-6-54-1.title: A catenary-shaped arch
pdf-figure-6-54-1.text: Hyperbolic functions describe the catenary curve associated with a hanging chain and related arch geometry.
pdf-figure-6-54-1.caption: A catenary-shaped arch

pdf-figure-6-54-2.title: Hyperbolic sine and cosine
pdf-figure-6-54-2.text: Combining positive and negative exponentials produces the hyperbolic functions.
pdf-figure-6-54-2.caption: Hyperbolic sine and cosine

pdf-figure-6-55-1.title: Circular and hyperbolic parametrizations
pdf-figure-6-55-1.text: Trigonometric and hyperbolic functions parametrize different geometric curves.
pdf-figure-6-55-1.caption: Circular and hyperbolic parametrizations

pdf-figure-7-4-1.title: Integration by parts as complementary areas
pdf-figure-7-4-1.text: The product can be divided into complementary accumulated contributions.
pdf-figure-7-4-1.caption: Integration by parts as complementary areas

pdf-figure-7-6-1.title: A variable force and displacement
pdf-figure-7-6-1.text: The force-displacement relation determines the work and motivates an integral calculation.
pdf-figure-7-6-1.caption: A variable force and displacement

pdf-figure-7-12-1.title: Trigonometric integrals in geometry
pdf-figure-7-12-1.text: Circular geometry and latitude bands lead to integrals involving trigonometric functions.
pdf-figure-7-12-1.caption: Trigonometric integrals in geometry

pdf-figure-7-14-1.title: Products of oscillations
pdf-figure-7-14-1.text: Multiplying oscillatory functions produces alternating contributions whose signs affect their integrals.
pdf-figure-7-14-1.caption: Products of oscillations

pdf-figure-7-15-1.title: Trigonometric substitution geometry
pdf-figure-7-15-1.text: A circular arc can be parametrized by an angle to simplify a square root.
pdf-figure-7-15-1.caption: Trigonometric substitution geometry

pdf-figure-7-16-1.title: Areas after substitution
pdf-figure-7-16-1.text: A substitution changes the expression while preserving the accumulated area represented by the integral.
pdf-figure-7-16-1.caption: Areas after substitution

pdf-figure-7-20-1.title: Triangles for radical substitutions
pdf-figure-7-20-1.text: A right triangle connects the chosen trigonometric substitution with the square root in the integrand.
pdf-figure-7-20-1.caption: Triangles for radical substitutions

pdf-figure-7-27-1.title: Improper areas
pdf-figure-7-27-1.text: An unbounded interval can enclose either a finite or an infinite total area.
pdf-figure-7-27-1.caption: Improper areas

pdf-figure-7-28-1.title: Convergence of power tails
pdf-figure-7-28-1.text: The rate of decay determines whether the area of a power-function tail converges.
pdf-figure-7-28-1.caption: Convergence of power tails

pdf-figure-7-30-1.title: Limits defining improper integrals
pdf-figure-7-30-1.text: Truncating an infinite interval gives finite integrals whose limiting behavior decides convergence.
pdf-figure-7-30-1.caption: Limits defining improper integrals

pdf-figure-8-2-1.title: Areas between curves
pdf-figure-8-2-1.text: The difference between upper and lower boundaries determines the height of each slice.
pdf-figure-8-2-1.caption: Areas between curves

pdf-figure-8-3-1.title: Integrating slices
pdf-figure-8-3-1.text: Different choices of slicing direction produce different but equivalent descriptions of area.
pdf-figure-8-3-1.caption: Integrating slices

pdf-figure-8-4-1.title: Choosing coordinates for area
pdf-figure-8-4-1.text: Expressing the boundaries in the slicing variable makes the area calculation possible.
pdf-figure-8-4-1.caption: Choosing coordinates for area

pdf-figure-8-5-1.title: Volumes by cross sections
pdf-figure-8-5-1.text: A solid's cross-sectional area varies along the axis and is accumulated to obtain volume.
pdf-figure-8-5-1.caption: Volumes by cross sections

pdf-figure-8-6-1.title: Disks and washers
pdf-figure-8-6-1.text: A cross section perpendicular to an axis of rotation can be a disk or a washer with a central hole.
pdf-figure-8-6-1.caption: Disks and washers

pdf-figure-8-7-1.title: Alternative volume decompositions
pdf-figure-8-7-1.text: Disks, washers and cylindrical layers describe the same volume through different decompositions.
pdf-figure-8-7-1.caption: Alternative volume decompositions

pdf-figure-8-9-1.title: Cylindrical shells
pdf-figure-8-9-1.text: Rotating a thin strip parallel to the axis creates a cylindrical shell.
pdf-figure-8-9-1.caption: Cylindrical shells

pdf-figure-8-10-1.title: Setting up geometric integrals
pdf-figure-8-10-1.text: The shape and orientation of a region determine convenient slices and their limits.
pdf-figure-8-10-1.caption: Setting up geometric integrals

pdf-figure-8-10-2.title: Sections of solids
pdf-figure-8-10-2.text: A diagram helps identify the radius, height or area needed for a volume integral.
pdf-figure-8-10-2.caption: Sections of solids

pdf-figure-8-12-1.title: Approximating arc length
pdf-figure-8-12-1.text: A small curve segment is approximated by a straight segment whose length follows from the Pythagorean theorem.
pdf-figure-8-12-1.caption: Approximating arc length

pdf-figure-8-12-2.title: Differential arc length
pdf-figure-8-12-2.text: Horizontal and vertical differentials combine to give the differential of curve length.
pdf-figure-8-12-2.caption: Differential arc length

pdf-figure-8-13-1.title: Polygonal approximations to a curve
pdf-figure-8-13-1.text: Adding lengths of short straight segments approaches the length of the curve.
pdf-figure-8-13-1.caption: Polygonal approximations to a curve

pdf-figure-8-13-2.title: Arc-length elements for different curves
pdf-figure-8-13-2.text: The derivative enters the length element through the local right triangle.
pdf-figure-8-13-2.caption: Arc-length elements for different curves

pdf-figure-8-17-1.title: Surface area of revolution
pdf-figure-8-17-1.text: Rotating a short arc creates a narrow band whose area depends on radius and arc length.
pdf-figure-8-17-1.caption: Surface area of revolution

pdf-figure-8-19-1.title: Unrolling a conical surface
pdf-figure-8-19-1.text: A cone's curved surface can be unrolled into a sector to calculate its area.
pdf-figure-8-19-1.caption: Unrolling a conical surface

pdf-figure-8-19-2.title: A narrow conical band
pdf-figure-8-19-2.text: The geometry of a frustum leads to the local area element used for surfaces of revolution.
pdf-figure-8-19-2.caption: A narrow conical band

pdf-figure-8-22-1.title: Probability densities
pdf-figure-8-22-1.text: The height of a density is related to the probability in a small interval through area.
pdf-figure-8-22-1.caption: Probability densities

pdf-figure-8-23-1.title: Density and cumulative probability
pdf-figure-8-23-1.text: Integrating a probability density gives the cumulative probability function.
pdf-figure-8-23-1.caption: Density and cumulative probability

pdf-figure-8-28-1.title: Masses and moments
pdf-figure-8-28-1.text: Weighted positions combine through moments to determine a system's center of mass.
pdf-figure-8-28-1.caption: Masses and moments

pdf-figure-8-30-1.title: Centroids of planar regions
pdf-figure-8-30-1.text: Symmetry and weighted area integrals determine the center of a uniform region.
pdf-figure-8-30-1.caption: Centroids of planar regions

pdf-figure-8-31-1.title: Centers of mass in physical objects
pdf-figure-8-31-1.text: The distribution of mass, rather than the outline alone, determines the center of mass.
pdf-figure-8-31-1.caption: Centers of mass in physical objects

pdf-figure-8-33-1.title: Centroids and rotational geometry
pdf-figure-8-33-1.text: The position of a centroid connects planar geometry with volumes generated by rotation.
pdf-figure-8-33-1.caption: Centroids and rotational geometry

pdf-figure-8-33-2.title: Volumes and weighted positions
pdf-figure-8-33-2.text: Cross-sectional areas and their locations determine both total volume and centroid.
pdf-figure-8-33-2.caption: Volumes and weighted positions

pdf-figure-8-36-1.title: Work in different force fields
pdf-figure-8-36-1.text: Springs, lifting and gravitational motion require integrating force along displacement.
pdf-figure-8-36-1.caption: Work in different force fields

pdf-figure-8-38-1.title: Work and fluid pressure
pdf-figure-8-38-1.text: The distance moved and the depth-dependent pressure determine the integrals for pumping and hydrostatic force.
pdf-figure-8-38-1.caption: Work and fluid pressure
